rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 report the authors' own greenhouse inoculation experiments (repeated twice), spectroradiometer measurements, a field experiment at Klein-Altendorf and hyperspectral imaging. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 3 report that the developed SDIs had higher classification accuracy than common SVIs (HI 89.0% vs NDVI 80.3% for healthy vs diseased; CLSI 92.4% vs NDVI 73.4% for Cercospora), with SVIs unsuitable (50%) for rust and powdery mildew identification; Section 3.4 and Fig. 5 report HI applied to canopy-scale field spectroradiometer data with 81.63% accuracy. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 2 measure the disease- and severity-specific changes in leaf reflectance (e.g. Cercospora raising VIS 500-700 nm and lowering NIR, powdery mildew raising overall reflectance), and Fig. 3 identifies the relevant wavelengths; these measured spectral changes are the intermediate through which the indices discriminate diseases. Q7: Section 3.4 and Discussion state that because of different light conditions and sensor specifications the classification threshold has to be optimized individually for each dataset prior to classification; results also show detection requires disease severity above a few percent (Table 2). Q8: Conclusion and Discussion state difficulties remained at early infection stages due to minor reflectance changes; Section 3.4 notes that mixed infections in the field made disease-specific classification unsuitable; the field/imaging application is described as a first feasibility study with further work needed on canopy and field scale.
rows.notes: The passage's claim of improved accuracy versus NDVI is supported by the study's own leaf-scale comparison under controlled greenhouse conditions (Table 3). The 'real world field conditions' part is only partly supported: the field application used only the health index (81.63%), was not compared with NDVI or other SVIs, and disease differentiation was not possible in the field owing to mixed infections. Q3 no: SDI-vs-SVI comparison rests on one method (cross-validated classification of spectroradiometer data against visual severity scores); the independent datasets are further applications of the same spectral approach. Q5 no: one crop, one cultivar, one greenhouse and one field site; the three diseases are not sites. Q6 no: the field test is a single research field. Q9 no: classification accuracies are reported without SD, CI or range; Fig. 2 standard deviations concern reflectance, not the detection-accuracy result. The function field is pest_control, but the passage itself claims detection accuracy, which the study addresses; the study has no result on disease control or management outcomes.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.6 report the authors' own greenhouse inoculation experiments, spectroradiometer measurements, a field experiment and hyperspectral imaging data.
rows.notes: The study shows only that spectral disease indices detect and differentiate sugar beet leaf diseases with higher classification accuracy than common vegetation indices (Tables 1-3) and can be applied to field and imaging data. It reports no yield, quality or crop production data and does not test whether improved detection leads to timely management or avoided losses; this is a precondition of the crop production effect, not evidence of it.

notes: Full text available (Remote Sensing of Environment 128, 2013, 21-30). Study is a methodological development of spectral disease indices for sugar beet leaf diseases under controlled conditions, with a small transferability test on one field dataset and hyperspectral images; no irrigation or yield component.
